items.title: Google Antigravity's /teamwork-preview lands alongside Gemini 4 Carbon's GA — a multi-agent mode that spawns a planner, specialist workers and auditors from a single prompt, gated to the $200 AI Ultra tier
items.summary: Alongside Gemini 4 Carbon's paid-API general availability on November 10 (covered in today's am), Google surfaced a second product worth tracking on its own: a research preview of Antigravity's multi-agent mode, invoked with the slash command /teamwork-preview. The pattern: a user sends a single prompt, a lead agent interviews the user and plans the work, then delegates to specialist worker agents and auditor agents that run asynchronously on hours-to-days-long tasks. Access is gated to Google AI Ultra subscribers (the $200/month tier) using Antigravity 2.0, and Google's own release materials warn that a single Teamwork session can exhaust the subscriber's entire weekly quota within a couple of tasks. Reported results from Google: a security audit that identified four previously unknown critical-severity bugs by tracing runtime permissions in a target codebase, and a separate math-and-engineering demo that produced a working CPU simulator. Sources disagree on which model powers the Teamwork agents — Google's own blog language ties Antigravity 2.0 to Gemini 4 Argon for AI Ultra subscribers, while at least one secondary write-up names Gemini 3.7 Flash as the underlying model for Teamwork specifically. That ambiguity will take a day or two to resolve as developer accounts work through real tasks. The underlying mechanism — a multi-agent swarm coordinated by one planning agent — is the first major-lab product to put the Scion-style testbed pattern (parallel agents with isolated identities and shared workspaces) behind a consumer-facing slash command in an IDE-adjacent surface.
items.why_it_matters: Teamwork is worth noticing even if you will not pay $200/month for it. Three reasons. First, it is the first major-lab product that puts multi-agent orchestration behind a user-facing slash command in a developer-adjacent surface. Everything before this — OpenAI Swarm, LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Google's own Scion testbed — is a framework you assemble yourself. Teamwork is the first time a frontier lab has shipped the assembly as a single feature. If the pattern catches on, expect Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the next generation of IDE plugins to carry a similar slash command within three to six months. Second, the planner-plus-workers-plus-auditors structure is worth understanding independently of the product, because it maps cleanly onto patterns Gabe can build in Python. The Agent SDK ships the hook-and-tool-call surface that would let you build a stripped-down version of this yourself: a top-level planner agent calls a worker agent for each step, and an auditor agent reviews the output. That is a small weekend project and a direct way to learn what a multi-agent loop actually costs in tokens and wall-time. Third, the quota warning is the one to carry forward. Google's own language — a single Teamwork session can exhaust the subscriber's weekly quota in a couple of tasks — is the clearest public signal yet from a frontier lab that multi-agent workloads are 10-100x the cost of a single-agent chat, and that pricing for agent workloads is going to look very different from the $20/month flat-rate pattern today. For a hobbyist, the practical version is: wait for a $20-tier equivalent to appear in the next 6-12 months, or build a tiny version on the Anthropic or Gemini API and measure the per-task cost yourself. The gating of Teamwork to the $200 tier is a signal that frontier labs now have a working concept of 'agent-grade workloads' that carry different pricing from chat.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 'Le Chonk' open weights have been on Hugging Face since October 29 — a 1-trillion-parameter model with 52B active, Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License, picking up fresh attention during Cursor transition week
items.summary: Mistral released the full weights of Mistral Large 4 — internally nicknamed 'Le Chonk' — on Hugging Face on October 29, 2026, under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (a modified MIT variant). The primary repository is mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B, with a separate NVFP4-quantized checkpoint published alongside. The architecture: approximately 1.05 trillion total parameters with around 52 billion active per token (sources disagree between 49B and 52B active; the model card lists 52B). Natively multimodal — image and text inputs supported. The item did not make the digest in the intervening days despite the date, and it is picking up fresh attention this week because developers evaluating replacement options for Cursor's OpenAI shutoff tomorrow are explicitly running coding comparisons against open-weight options. Reported benchmarks: Mistral itself reports a 48% score on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, which Mistral frames as effectively tied with the leading open-weight model (GLM-5.3), while using 47% fewer tokens per task. A separate secondary report cites 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (up 13 points from the preview) and a 19.7% score on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark — the FrontierCode number is vendor-aggregator-reported rather than from Mistral or Cognition directly. Hardware requirements: approximately 1 TB in FP8 precision, or approximately 580 GB in NVFP4 quantization — self-hostable only on serious GPU budgets. The licensing terms are the most permissive among the current trillion-parameter open-weight tier: no revenue thresholds, no field-of-use restrictions, trademark retained.
items.why_it_matters: This is a catch-up item that is worth putting into the snapshot during Cursor-transition week specifically. Over the next 7-10 days, developer teams running Cursor are picking replacement providers — Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, SpaceXAI Grok, or an open-weight stack. Mistral Large 4 is the strongest EU-based option in that evaluation, and it did not surface in the am file today. Three threads matter. First, the licensing structure is the one real differentiator against the Chinese open-weight stack. The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License is close to MIT (no revenue thresholds, no field-of-use restrictions), which lets a hobbyist wrap the model in a side project or a commercial tool without worrying about the kind of compete-with-DeepSeek clauses that make the DeepSeek R2 license more restrictive. Second, the token-efficiency claim — 47% fewer tokens per task at equivalent coding-agent-index score — is the specific capability lane that matters for agentic workflows. Coding agents are token-bound before they are quality-bound; a model that does the same task in half the tokens is substantially cheaper at scale, and that compounds in long tool-use sequences. If independent benchmarks confirm the claim, Mistral Large 4 is the strongest open-weight option for anyone building a long-running coding agent. Third, the hardware constraint is the honest one: 1 TB in FP8 means self-hosting requires 10-12 top-end datacenter GPUs. The quantized checkpoint drops that to about 580 GB — still well above a consumer workstation. For Gabe, this is not a self-host candidate without a cloud rental, but it is a viable API-based option via Mistral's La Plateforme, Together AI, Fireworks, and other open-model hosts. The Cursor shutoff tomorrow is a reminder that model-access decisions are now portfolio decisions: keeping a third viable provider configured (alongside Anthropic and Google) is a small amount of work for a significant resilience gain if any of the major providers has a termination event like the one Cursor is facing.

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit runs Nov 10-12 in San Francisco — the second annual single-track summit on coding agents, with Databricks' Ankit Mathur and Cognition's Walden Yan on the speaker list; developer announcements likely to time with the three-day window
items.summary: The AI Engineer Code Summit, the second annual edition of swyx's application-only single-track summit on coding agents, is running November 10-12, 2026 at the Hilton San Francisco Union Square. Program format: November 10 is a workshop day, and November 11-12 are two full days of single-track keynotes and sessions alongside a Summit Expo and an afterparty. The focus is explicitly coding agents, code review, and internal agents — the summit's framing is developer-tools engineers and the teams running agentic workflows in production at companies like Ramp and Coinbase. Confirmed speakers include Databricks' Ankit Mathur and Cognition co-founder Walden Yan. The broader lineup was not fully published as of this snapshot and the official schedule page notes that program details are still being assembled. The week-long context is dense: the summit overlaps with Cursor's OpenAI-model shutoff on November 12 (final day of the summit), the Antigravity Teamwork research preview rolling out on the Gemini 4 Carbon GA day, Claude Code's November release train, and NVIDIA's CoRL 2026 week. Developer-tooling announcements traditionally cluster around this summit — expect new MCP server releases, agent-framework updates, and at least one or two new model releases timed to land during the three-day window. The Nov 11 program is Wednesday, the first of the two full-day sessions.
items.why_it_matters: This is a Tier-3 scene-setting item, not a specific announcement. Three things make it worth documenting. First, the Code Summit is now the single most important venue for developer-tooling announcements in the AI-coding-agent space — in a way that the AI Engineer World's Fair in June covers the broader applied-AI audience. For anyone tracking Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Devin, Aider, OpenHands, or any of the newer agentic-coding tools, the summit is where the practical patterns and the next tool releases surface. The 2025 edition in NYC produced several of the current patterns around hook-based agent guardrails and multi-model routing — the same themes Anthropic's November Claude Code release train is now productizing. Expect the 2026 Code Summit to similarly seed the patterns we will see in Cursor's post-OpenAI stack, Codex CLI's next release, and Claude Code's v2.2 series. Second, the summit's timing — overlapping with the Cursor shutoff on its final day — gives it a specific journalistic weight this year. The engineers running Cursor's migration lane, and the teams building replacement IDEs or CLI tools, are in the room together for three days during the transition. Expect the panel discussions and hallway-track exchanges to produce the next 6 months of 'how do you actually structure a coding-agent stack' guidance. Third, for a hobbyist, the practical version is: follow the summit's Latent Space podcast episodes (swyx runs both) over the next 7-10 days. The talks will land on YouTube on a 1-3 week lag, but the podcast coverage and swyx's own writeups will surface the key patterns immediately. If any new developer tool, MCP server, or coding-agent framework is announced at the summit, it will show up in next week's digest cycle with the real-world engineering reactions already attached.
